method_card.title: Range, Quartiles and Interquartile Range
method_card.content:
Averages tell us about the centre of a distribution, but they say nothing about how spread out the data are. Two datasets can have the same mean yet very different spreads. We use measures of spread to capture this.

The range is the simplest: \(\text{Range} = \text{Maximum} - \text{Minimum}\). It is easy to calculate but sensitive to outliers.

The quartiles divide an ordered dataset into four equal parts. \(Q_1\) (lower quartile) is the median of the lower half; \(Q_2\) is the median of all the data; \(Q_3\) (upper quartile) is the median of the upper half. The specification ensures exam datasets have \(n\) values where \(n\) is one less than a multiple of 4 (e.g. 7, 11, 15, 19), so quartile positions are always whole numbers and no interpolation is needed. For \(n = 4k - 1\): \(Q_1\) is at position \(k\), \(Q_2\) is at position \(2k\), \(Q_3\) is at position \(3k\).

The interquartile range (IQR) measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data: \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\). Because it ignores the top and bottom 25% of values, the IQR is not affected by outliers — making it more informative than the range when outliers are present.

For identifying outliers by calculation (Higher): a value is an outlier if it is more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) above \(Q_3\) or more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) below \(Q_1\). The 1.5 × IQR rule is given in the Higher formula sheet.
steps: Order the data from smallest to largest
Find the median (\(Q_2\)) using the \(\frac{n+1}{2}\) position rule
Find \(Q_1\) at position \(k\) and \(Q_3\) at position \(3k\) where \(n = 4k - 1\)
For outlier detection (Higher): check whether any value is more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) beyond \(Q_1\) or \(Q_3\)

exam_context.marks: 1–2 marks for range or IQR; 2–3 marks for finding both quartiles; up to 2 marks for outlier identification
exam_context.frequency: High frequency; quartile and IQR questions appear on nearly every paper, often as part of a box plot or comparative distributions question

worked_examples.question: Find Q1 and Q3 for the ordered dataset: 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13.

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify n and quartile positions
steps.content: \(n = 7 = 4(2) - 1\), so \(k = 2\). \(Q_1\) is at position 2. \(Q_3\) is at position 6.

worked_examples.question: A dataset of 11 values (ordered): 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 27, 30, 55. Find Q1, Q3, IQR, and determine whether 55 is an outlier using the 1.5 × IQR rule.

steps.label: Step 2 — Apply the outlier rule
steps.content:
Upper fence \(= Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 27 + 1.5 \times 19 = 27 + 28.5 = 55.5\).

Is 55 above the upper fence? \(55 < 55.5\), so 55 is NOT an outlier.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: \(Q_1 = 8\), \(Q_3 = 27\), IQR = 19. Upper fence = 55.5. Since 55 < 55.5, the value 55 is not an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule.

misconceptions.message: Count the values: 4, 7, 9, 11, 14, 17, 20 — that is 7 values. n = 7.

bronze.display: A dataset of 7 ordered values has k = 2. At which position is Q1?

misconceptions.message: For n = 4k − 1, Q1 is at position k. With k = 2, Q1 is the 2nd value in the ordered list.

bronze.display: Find Q3 in the ordered list: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13.

misconceptions.message: n = 7 = 4(2) − 1, k = 2. Q3 is at position 3k = 6. The 6th value is 11.

bronze.display: Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 28. What is the IQR?
Find Q1 and Q3 for the ordered list: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21.

misconceptions.message: n = 7 = 4(2) − 1, k = 2. Q1 is the 2nd value = 6. Q3 is the 6th value = 18.

bronze.display: A distribution has Q1 = 15, Q2 = 22, Q3 = 31. What percentage of the data lies between Q1 and Q3?

misconceptions.message: Q1 and Q3 mark the 25th and 75th percentiles. The interval between them contains the middle 50% of the data.

bronze.display: Which measure of spread is least affected by outliers?
options: Range
IQR
Mean
Mode

misconceptions.message: The IQR only uses the middle 50% of data (Q1 to Q3), so it is not affected by extreme values. The range is directly affected by outliers because it uses the maximum and minimum.

silver.display: An ordered dataset of 11 values: 2, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 25, 28, 32. Find Q1 and Q3.

misconceptions.message: n = 11 = 4(3) − 1, k = 3. Q1 is at position 3 = 7. Q3 is at position 9 = 25.

silver.display: An ordered dataset of 15 values has Q1 at position k and Q3 at position 3k. What is k?

misconceptions.message: n = 15 = 4k − 1 ⇒ 4k = 16 ⇒ k = 4. Q1 is at position 4, Q3 is at position 12.

silver.display: A dataset has IQR = 14 and Q1 = 20. What is Q3?

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1. So Q3 = IQR + Q1 = 14 + 20 = 34.

silver.display: Two datasets both have mean 25. Dataset A has IQR = 4. Dataset B has IQR = 18. What does this tell us about the two distributions?
options: Dataset A is more spread out than Dataset B
Dataset B is more spread out than Dataset A
They have the same spread because their means are equal
Dataset B must contain more data points than Dataset A

misconceptions.message: A higher IQR means the middle 50% of data covers a wider range. Dataset B (IQR = 18) is more spread out than Dataset A (IQR = 4), even though both datasets have the same mean.

silver.display: An ordered dataset of 19 values: the 5th value is 13 and the 15th value is 41. What is the IQR?

misconceptions.message: n = 19 = 4(5) − 1, k = 5. Q1 is at position 5 = 13. Q3 is at position 15 = 41. IQR = 41 − 13 = 28.

silver.display: A dataset (ordered): 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30. Calculate the range and IQR.

misconceptions.message: Range = 30 − 6 = 24. For IQR: n=7, k=2. Q1 (position 2) = 10. Q3 (position 6) = 26. IQR = 26 − 10 = 16. Make sure you give both answers.

gold.display: A dataset of 11 values (ordered): 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 80. Determine whether 80 is an outlier using the 1.5 × IQR rule.
options: Yes, 80 is an outlier because it is above the upper fence
No, 80 is not an outlier because it is within the upper fence
The 1.5 × IQR rule cannot be applied to this dataset
Yes, 80 is an outlier because it is the maximum value

misconceptions.message: n=11, k=3. Q1 (position 3) = 12. Q3 (position 9) = 36. IQR = 24. Upper fence = 36 + 1.5(24) = 36 + 36 = 72. Since 80 > 72, it IS an outlier.

gold.display: A dataset of 7 values has Q1 = 10, Q3 = 22. A new value of 44 is added, making n = 8. Without the outlier rule, is 44 an outlier by inspection?
options: Yes, because it is more than double Q3
No, because the outlier rule requires calculation
It depends on the mean of the dataset
Yes, because it is the maximum value

misconceptions.message: Outlier 'by inspection' means identifying a value that appears dramatically out of step with the rest of the data. 44 is far above Q3 = 22 and clearly separated from the main cluster. You don't need to apply the 1.5 × IQR rule for inspection.

gold.display: Dataset A (ordered, n=7): 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29. Dataset B (ordered, n=7): 12, 14, 16, 17, 18, 20, 22. Both have median 17. Which dataset is more consistent and why?
options: Dataset A, because it has a larger range of values
Dataset B, because it has a smaller IQR
Dataset A, because its values are evenly spaced
Both are equally consistent because they share the same median

misconceptions.message: Dataset A: Q1=9, Q3=25, IQR=16. Dataset B: Q1=14, Q3=20, IQR=6. A smaller IQR means the middle 50% of data is more tightly clustered, indicating greater consistency. Dataset B is more consistent.

gold.display: A dataset (ordered, n=11): 2, 4, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 45, 90. Apply the 1.5 × IQR rule. Which values (if any) are outliers?
options: 90 only
45 and 90
No values are outliers
2 only

misconceptions.message: n=11, k=3. Q1 (position 3) = 7. Q3 (position 9) = 31. IQR = 24. Upper fence = 31 + 36 = 67. Lower fence = 7 − 36 = −29. 90 > 67 so 90 IS an outlier. 45 < 67 so 45 is NOT an outlier. 2 > −29 so not an outlier. Only 90 is an outlier.

gold.display: A dataset of 7 values has IQR = 20. A value at the upper quartile is 35. What is the lower quartile?

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1. So Q1 = Q3 − IQR = 35 − 20 = 15.
